## Abstract {.unnumbered}

The Steamboat Hills geothermal system, south of Reno, Nevada, has been
studied since the 1950s and produced commercially since the 1980s, but
its surface expression has not been static: natural hot-spring flow at
the Lower Sinter Terrace declined and ceased between 1986 and 1989, had
still not resumed by 2000, and then, beginning around 2022, began
reawakening, culminating in a geyser-like eruption on June 3, 2025.
This proposal describes a relational geodatabase and analysis pipeline
built to support a thesis investigating that reawakening along three
lines: whether the thermal-water outflow chemistry has genuinely
changed since Michael Sorey's foundational studies, whether continuous
specific-conductance monitoring can substitute for costly discrete
chloride sampling as a proxy for thermal-water discharge, and what the
subsurface plumbing feeding the terrace looks like. The database
currently integrates field, state-agency, federal, and historical-
literature chemistry and hydrologic data spanning 1950 through 2026,
with a documented quality-control process, geochemical (PHREEQC)
modeling capability, and a Monte Carlo-informed sampling-frequency
analysis. Real findings to date include a statistically detectable but
small shift in the thermal end-member's conservative chloride-to-boron
ratio, a systematic divergence between two independent geothermometers
consistent with a single cooling and diluting flow path, three
independent statistical methods converging on the same hydrochemical
facies structure, and a real, database-computed thermal-water discharge
estimate. The proposal closes with a concrete calibration chloride-
sampling plan, a data request that would unblock a real potentiometric
surface, and a scoped path toward a fault-informed, Leapfrog-based
three-dimensional geologic model -- the specific, sequenced steps
remaining before this thesis's three central questions can be fully
answered.
